stati.risposta: Yes: as of {data}, Utah law lets you plug in a solar device of up to 1,200 watts without your utility's approval or any fee, under H.B. 340, in force since May 7, 2025.

legge_punti.t: H.B. 340, "Solar Power Amendments", passed in the 2025 General Session; the governor signed it on March 25, 2025.
It took effect on May 7, 2025. It added Utah Code 54-15-601 and a definition of "portable solar generation device" in 54-15-102.
The Utah Code site lists the 2025 text of 54-15-601 as the current version.

limiti.t: Maximum power output: 1,200 watts, through a standard 120-volt AC outlet.
The device must meet the latest National Electrical Code and be certified by UL or an equivalent nationally recognized testing laboratory.
It must include a feature that stops it from energizing the building's wiring during a power outage.
The utility may not require its approval, a fee, or equipment beyond what is built into the device. The law does not mention a notice to the utility.
The device is outside net metering, and the utility is not liable for damage or injury it causes.

condo.t: H.B. 340 does not mention condominium associations, HOAs or landlords: it limits what the utility can require, not what your association's rules say.
Because the law is silent on associations, read your declaration, bylaws and rules, and ask the board in writing before you buy a kit.

faq.q: What is the balcony solar law in Utah?
faq.a: It is H.B. 340 of 2025, now Utah Code 54-15-601. Since May 7, 2025, a certified plug-in solar device of up to 1,200 watts that plugs into a standard 120-volt outlet needs no interconnection agreement, no utility approval and no fee. The law says nothing about condominium or HOA rules.

stati.risposta: Yes: as of {data}, Colorado law allows plug-in solar devices of up to 1,920 watts with no utility approval or fee, and from January 1, 2027 a condo or HOA cannot unreasonably prohibit them (HB26-1007, in force since August 12, 2026).

legge_punti.t: HB26-1007, "Improve Customer Use Distributed Energy Resources", became law: the governor signed it on May 7, 2026.
It is Chapter 127 of the 2026 Session Laws, with an effective date of August 12, 2026. It adds section 40-2-140 to the Colorado Revised Statutes.

limiti.t: One photovoltaic system per address, designed to supply at most 1,920 watts to the grid, labeled and listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.
No more than one device on a single wall outlet per address, and a feature that stops it from energizing the grid during an outage.
The utility may not require its approval, a fee or extra equipment. It may ask you to tell it that you use a device and its size in kilowatts.

Devices of 391 watts or less are exempt from code or listing provisions that would require changes to the building's wiring. From January 1, 2027, devices above 391 watts that are not UL labeled and listed may not be sold, leased or rented in Colorado.
Installation must follow fire code requirements and local building codes on health and safety.

condo.t: From January 1, 2027, a covenant or restriction that unreasonably prohibits or restricts a plug-in device is void, and the device counts as an "energy efficiency measure" under the common interest community law (CRS 38-33.3-106.7).
An owner may install and use a device on a limited common element, such as a balcony, patio or deck that serves only the owner's unit.

The association may require the owner to secure the device reasonably to the unit or to that balcony, patio or deck. The owner may be responsible for the costs and liability of installation, maintenance and removal, and may have to indemnify the association and other owners.
Reasonable restrictions remain possible, for example prior notice, rules to prevent fire or electrical overload, and the location of the device.

faq.q: What does Colorado's balcony solar law say?
faq.a: HB26-1007, signed on May 7, 2026 and in force since August 12, 2026, lets a customer use one plug-in solar system per address of up to 1,920 watts without utility approval or fees; the utility may ask for a notice of the device and its size. From January 1, 2027, condo and HOA rules cannot unreasonably prohibit these devices, but reasonable restrictions on notice, safety and location are allowed.

stati.risposta: Yes: as of {data}, Maine law allows plug-in solar and plug-in battery systems at home, up to 420 watts with no notice and up to 1,200 watts with a licensed electrician and a notice to the utility (LD 1730, Public Law 2026, Chapter 644).

legge_punti.t: LD 1730 (SP 676), "An Act to Make Small Plug-in Solar Generation Devices Accessible for All Maine Residents", was enacted and signed by the governor on April 6, 2026, as Chapter 644 of the Public Laws.
It adds section 3475 to Title 35-A. The law has no emergency clause, and the Legislature gives July 29, 2026 as the general effective date for non-emergency laws of that session.

limiti.t: Eligible systems have an export capacity of 1,200 watts or less and are listed or certified under UL 3700 or a comparable standard, or configured under the National Electrical Code adopted in Maine.
Up to 420 watts of combined inverter output per service address: no notice is needed.

From 420 to 1,200 watts: each system must be installed by a Maine-licensed electrician on a dedicated circuit with a single outlet, and you must notify the utility within 30 days on the form set by the Public Utilities Commission.
The utility may not require approval, an interconnection application, a fee or extra equipment, and may not deny a system that follows the law. The system cannot be used for net energy billing.

condo.t: Chapter 644 does not mention condominium associations or HOAs.

If you install a system on a structure you do not own, you must make sure it does not compromise the structure or break building, fire or zoning codes, and you must restore the structure when you remove the system.

faq.q: What is Maine's balcony solar law?
faq.a: It is LD 1730, Public Law 2026, Chapter 644, signed on April 6, 2026. You may use plug-in solar or battery systems of up to 420 watts per service address without notice; between 420 and 1,200 watts, a licensed electrician must install each system on a dedicated circuit and you must notify the utility within 30 days.

stati.risposta: Yes: as of {data}, Maryland law allows one portable solar system of up to 1,200 watts per electric meter for residential use, with a notice to your utility before you install it (Public Utilities § 7-321, from HB 1532 of 2026).

legge_punti.t: HB 1532, the Utility RELIEF Act, was approved by the governor on May 12, 2026 as Chapter 353. Among many energy measures it adds § 7-321 to the Public Utilities Article.
The Department of Legislative Services gives July 1, 2026 as the effective date of the portable solar provisions.

limiti.t: A movable system that plugs into a standard outlet, supplies at most 1,200 watts back to the building's electric system and is certified by UL or an equivalent laboratory.
Not more than one system per electric meter, for residential use only.

You must notify your electric company before installation and give it a certification of the system's safety features and maximum capacity. If the system requires an automatic locking disconnect switch, you pay for its installation.

The utility may not require approval, a fee for feeding power back, or other extra equipment. Systems of 391 watts or less are exempt from listing provisions that would require changes to wiring or panels.

condo.t: § 7-321 does not mention condominium associations, HOAs or landlords.
Your association's declaration, bylaws and rules therefore still matter: ask the board in writing before you place a panel on a balcony or railing.

faq.q: What is the balcony solar law in Maryland?
faq.a: It is § 7-321 of the Public Utilities Article, added by HB 1532 (Chapter 353 of 2026). You may install one portable solar system of up to 1,200 watts per meter for residential use, after notifying the electric company and certifying the system's safety features and maximum capacity.

stati.risposta: Yes: as of {data}, Vermont law allows plug-in solar devices with up to 1,200 watts per electric meter, and condo or HOA covenants may not prohibit them (Act 149 of 2026, in force since July 1, 2026).

legge_punti.t: S.202 became Act 149, "An act relating to plug-in photovoltaic devices". The governor signed it on June 16, 2026, and it took effect on July 1, 2026.
It adds 30 V.S.A. § 256 and amends the rules on zoning bylaws (24 V.S.A. § 4413) and on deed restrictions and covenants (27 V.S.A. § 544).

limiti.t: One or more devices per electric meter with a maximum combined inverter capacity of 1,200 watts, plugged into a receptacle, certified under UL 3700 or an equivalent.
Devices may only be connected to systems with smart meters, must be temporarily but securely attached to the ground or a structure, and must stop energizing the building during an outage.
The utility may not require approval, a fee or extra controls, but may recover costs if a device overloads the service.
A customer with net metering may not also install a plug-in device, and power sent to the grid is not paid for.

condo.t: Deed restrictions, covenants and similar binding agreements may not prohibit, or have the effect of prohibiting, renewable energy devices; for plug-in devices this covers devices appurtenant to the buildings.
The exception for patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives and apartments does not apply to plug-in photovoltaic devices.

Tenants must give the landlord at least 10 days' notice. The landlord may answer within 10 days with reasonable restrictions; without an answer, the tenant may go ahead. Electrical work needs the landlord's permission.
Town zoning bylaws may not regulate the installation, operation and maintenance of plug-in devices.

faq.q: What is Vermont's balcony solar law?
faq.a: It is Act 149 of 2026 (S.202), in force since July 1, 2026. You may use plug-in solar devices with up to 1,200 watts of combined inverter capacity per meter, on a smart meter, without utility approval or fees. Covenants may not prohibit them, and the condo patio-railing exception does not apply to plug-in devices.

stati.risposta: Yes, from January 1, 2027: as of {data}, Virginia law (Code § 56-596.8, enacted in 2026) will allow plug-in solar devices of up to 1,200 watts per customer, or per unit in multifamily housing, after a notice to the utility.

legge_punti.t: Code of Virginia § 56-596.8, "Small portable solar generation devices; exempt from interconnection", takes effect on January 1, 2027.
Its history note cites 2026 Acts of Assembly chapters 998 and 1052.

limiti.t: Maximum output of 1,200 watts per customer, or per residential unit in multifamily housing; connected through an electrical outlet; certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory; meeting the latest National Electrical Code.

Before installing, you must notify the utility using the form set by the State Corporation Commission. The utility has 15 days to review it; if it does not answer, the notice requirement counts as met.
No utility approval, fee or extra equipment, but the utility may install an automatic locking disconnect switch where a property has more than one device or the circuit requires it.

Devices of 391 watts or less are exempt from listing provisions that would require changes to wiring or panels. The section does not apply to rental units billed through a ratio utility billing system.

condo.t: § 56-596.8 does not mention condominium unit owners' associations or property owners' associations.
The 1,200-watt limit is counted per residential unit in multifamily housing, so each condo unit has its own limit.

faq.q: What is Virginia's balcony solar law?
faq.a: It is § 56-596.8 of the Code of Virginia, effective January 1, 2027 (2026 Acts of Assembly chapters 998 and 1052). A device of up to 1,200 watts per customer, or per unit in multifamily housing, needs no interconnection, approval or fee, but you must notify the utility on the State Corporation Commission's form before installing it.

stati.risposta: Probably yes, from 2027: as of {data}, the Garden State Balcony Solar Act (S2368) would allow plug-in devices of up to 1,200 watts and bar condo associations from banning them, and a third-party tracker reports it was signed on September 1, 2026, but we could not confirm the signature on the Legislature's site.

legge_punti.t: S2368, the "Garden State Balcony Solar Act", was reported by the Assembly Budget Committee on June 28, 2026 (third reprint), identical to Assembly Bill 4836.
The bill says it takes effect six months after enactment.
The Legislature's status page needs JavaScript and we could not read the final votes. Bright Saver's tracker lists it as signed on September 1, 2026, effective March 1, 2027.

limiti.t: A device of up to 1,200 watts that plugs into a standard 120-volt outlet, is listed or certified under UL 3700 or a comparable standard, and stops exporting power during an outage.
The combined output at one service address, or at one dwelling unit in multifamily housing, may not exceed 1,200 watts without an interconnection agreement.
Utilities may not require approval, a fee or extra equipment. Devices of 400 watts or less are exempt from code provisions that would require changes to wiring or panels.
Municipalities may not prohibit the devices on residential property or require a permit or fee for placing them.

condo.t: A condominium association, HOA or cooperative may not enforce a master deed, bylaw or rule that prohibits a unit owner or tenant from using a device or placing it on the exterior of their premises; such provisions are void.
The association may set reasonable restrictions on size, placement and manner of placement, and may require indemnification for damage caused by negligent installation, maintenance or use.

A tenant who pays for the unit's electricity must give written notice to the landlord and to the association at least 14 days before placing or using a device, with documentation and the proposed location.

faq.q: Is balcony solar legal in New Jersey?
faq.ricerca: is balcony solar legal in new jersey
faq.a: The Garden State Balcony Solar Act (S2368) would allow certified plug-in devices of up to 1,200 watts per address or dwelling unit and stop condo and HOA rules from banning them, with reasonable restrictions allowed. It takes effect six months after enactment. A third-party tracker reports it was signed on September 1, 2026; we could not confirm this on the Legislature's site.

faq.q: Can New Jersey renters use balcony solar?
faq.a: Under S2368, a landlord may not prohibit a tenant who pays for the unit's electricity from using a device inside the leased premises, including a leased balcony or patio. The tenant must give written notice at least 14 days before, and the landlord may set reasonable restrictions on size and placement.

faq_indice.q: Can I put solar panels on my balcony?
faq_indice.ricerca: can i put solar panels on my balcony
faq_indice.a: It depends on two sets of rules: your state's law on plug-in devices and your building's rules. Even where the state law protects plug-in solar, condo and HOA rules on balconies and railings can still apply unless the law limits them, as Colorado's law does from January 1, 2027 and Vermont's law does for covenants. Ask your association in writing before you buy.

faq_indice.q: Can an HOA prevent solar panels on a balcony?
faq_indice.a: Among the laws we read, Colorado (from January 1, 2027) voids covenants that unreasonably prohibit plug-in devices, and Vermont's law stops covenants from prohibiting them, including on condo patio railings. New Jersey's S2368 text bars condo and HOA rules that ban them. Utah, Maine, Maryland and Virginia's plug-in laws do not mention associations, so your association's rules still matter there.

We cannot judge the safety of a product or of your wiring; ask a licensed electrician. What the laws require is clear: a device certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (UL 3700 is named in Maine, Vermont and New Jersey) and a feature that stops it from sending power during an outage. Maine requires a licensed electrician and a dedicated circuit above 420 watts.

faq_indice.q: Do you need an electrician for plug-in solar?
faq_indice.ricerca: do you need an electrician for plug in solar
faq_indice.a: Among the laws we read, only Maine requires one: systems with combined output above 420 watts, up to 1,200 watts, must be installed by a Maine-licensed electrician on a dedicated circuit with a single outlet. Elsewhere the laws do not require one for a device that simply plugs in, but any change to wiring follows the electrical code. For questions about your outlet or panel, ask a licensed electrician.

Vermont's law lets a tenant install after giving the landlord 10 days' notice, unless the landlord answers with reasonable restrictions. New Jersey's S2368 text stops landlords from banning devices for tenants who pay their own electricity, with 14 days' written notice. North Carolina's HB 1129, still a bill, would do something similar for larger landlords.

faq_indice.q: Do I have to notify my utility about plug-in solar?
faq_indice.a: It depends on the state. Maryland and Virginia require a notice before you install; Maine requires one within 30 days for systems above 420 watts; Colorado lets the utility ask for one. Utah's law does not mention a notice. Check your utility's website for its form.

faq_indice.q: Is balcony solar legal in Texas?
faq_indice.ricerca: is balcony solar legal in texas
faq_indice.a: Texas has no plug-in solar law that we could find. A third-party tracker lists no Texas bill as of the 2026 session, so the usual rules of your electric utility and your condo or HOA apply. Ask your utility before connecting anything that sends power into your home's wiring.
